data.context: The malware itself, a Windows DLL library, is typically saved to the local Windows folder as perfc.dat if it runs with SeDebugPrivilege permission.

evidence.quote: The malware itself, a Windows DLL library

data.context: If it does not have this privilege, it saves perfc.dat to the All Users application data directory (CSIDL_COMMON_APPDATA) which is resolved by Windows to either C:\ProgramData or 'C:\Documents and Settings\All Users\Application Data'.

evidence.quote: saves perfc.dat

data.context: The malware must be executed with a direct call to its export of ordinal 1, seen as '#1' in the command line.

evidence.quote: executed with a direct call to its export of ordinal 1

data.context: There are various reasons why malware tends to use this style of execution, with the most common being to prevent execution within a sandbox.

evidence.quote: malware tends to use this style of execution

data.context: Ransomware Data Encryption Upon execution, the malware will begin to perform privilege checking to determine what permissions the running account has, primarily checking for the SeDebugPrivilege permission, as detailed later in User Rights Checking and Malware Logic.

evidence.quote: Data Encryption Upon execution

data.context: If the running user has the SeDebugPrivilege permission, the malware will assume it has administrative privileges, it will then attempt to encrypt the drive using the known Petya code.

evidence.quote: it will then attempt to encrypt the drive using the known Petya code.

data.context: This is performed by overwriting the Master Boot Record (MBR) of the hard drive (PhysicalDrive0) with malicious code that displays a fake 'chkdsk.exe' partition repair screen as it encrypts the hard drive, shown below.

evidence.quote: overwriting the Master Boot Record (MBR) of the hard drive (PhysicalDrive0) with malicious code

data.context: This is a technique that is known to exist in Petya, using nearly identical text and code.

evidence.quote: using nearly identical text and code

data.context: This is the reason why the malware was initially considered to be Petya upon dynamic analysis, although static analysis showed vastly different code for the remainder of the malware's functionality.

evidence.quote: vastly different code for the remainder of the malware's functionality

data.context: MBR-based Ransom Note Alternatively, if the user is not running with administrative privileges, as determined by a lack of SeDebugPrivilege, the malware will use a user-space encryption routine, which is a different routine from the one detailed above.

evidence.quote: as determined by a lack of SeDebugPrivilege, the malware will use a user-space encryption routine

data.context: Like other recent malware the ransomware utilizes the highly effective EternalBlue exploit for Windows SMB vulnerabilities to copy itself to other systems and execute, which is detailed later in this post.

data.context: In addition to the SMB exploit propagation method, the malware also attempts to establish default administrative network shares (Admin$) with a call to WNetAddConnection2() using a null username and password.

data.context: By using null for these two values, the network connection is made using the current user's credentials, which directly affect organizations with shared local administrator accounts.

data.context: If a connection is made to the remote system, the malware will create a copy of itself directly on the other system using standard CreateFile() and WriteFile() API routines.
